title: Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP)

hero.subtitle: Bootstrap Protocol for automatic IP configuration of diskless workstations

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) was designed to allow diskless client machines to discover their own IP address, the address of a server host, and the name of a file to be loaded into memory and executed. It provides a foundation for automatic network configuration that preceded DHCP.

BOOTP was the successor to RARP (Reverse ARP) and provided significantly more configuration information. It was eventually superseded by DHCP (RFC 2131), which added dynamic address allocation.

Purpose
Allow diskless clients to obtain IP configuration at boot time without manual intervention.
Transport
Uses UDP with well-known ports: server port 67, client port 68.
sections.plainLanguage: The Bootstrap Protocol (BOOTP) lets a diskless client find its own IP address, a server's address, and the name of a file to load and run. It runs over UDP, with server port 67 and client port 68. BOOTP succeeded RARP and gave much more configuration information. DHCP (RFC 2131) later superseded it.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
BOOTP uses a single packet exchange model. The client broadcasts a BOOTREQUEST message, and the server responds with a BOOTREPLY containing the client's assigned IP address and boot parameters.

Feature
RARP
BOOTP
Protocol
Link layer
UDP/IP
Info Provided
IP only
IP + server + boot file
Router Traversal
No
Yes (relay agents)

The client identifies itself using its hardware address. The server maintains a static table mapping hardware addresses to IP assignments, ensuring consistent address allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: BOOTP uses a single exchange. The client broadcasts a BOOTREQUEST, and the server replies with a BOOTREPLY containing the client's IP address and boot parameters. The client identifies itself by its hardware address, and the server looks it up in a static table. Unlike RARP, BOOTP runs over UDP and IP, returns a server and boot file too, and can cross routers through relay agents.

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content: The BOOTP packet is carried in the data portion of a UDP datagram. It uses a fixed-format header followed by a vendor-specific area. The same layout is used in both directions, and the whole packet is 300 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: A BOOTP packet travels in the data part of a UDP datagram. It has a fixed-format header followed by a vendor-specific area. The same layout is used in both directions, and the whole packet is 300 bytes.

sections.title: Relay Agents
sections.content:
A key advantage of BOOTP over RARP is the ability to operate across network boundaries using relay agents (also known as BOOTP forwarders). This allows a single centralized BOOTP server to serve multiple network segments.

Relay agents listen for requests on the BOOTP server port (67) and forward requests to servers on remote networks. The giaddr field is filled in by the relay agent with the address of the interface on which the request was received, so the server knows which gateway to send the reply back through.

The relay agent process works as follows:

Step 1
Client broadcasts BOOTREQUEST on local subnet.
Step 2
Relay agent receives broadcast and inserts its address in giaddr field.
Step 3
Relay agent unicasts the request to the configured BOOTP server.
Step 4
Server sends BOOTREPLY to the relay agent, which forwards it to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay agent (BOOTP forwarder) lets one central server serve many network segments. It listens on server port 67, adds the address of the interface the request arrived on in the giaddr field, and unicasts the request to the BOOTP server. The server replies to the relay agent, which forwards the reply to the client.

sections.title: Vendor Extensions
sections.content:
BOOTP includes a 64-byte vendor-specific area that can carry additional configuration parameters. This extensibility mechanism was later formalized as BOOTP options and became the foundation for DHCP options.

Subnet MaskTag 1 - Client subnet mask
Default GatewayTag 3 - Router address for the client
DNS ServerTag 6 - Domain name server address
HostnameTag 12 - Client hostname
Domain NameTag 15 - Domain name for client resolution

The original 64-byte vendor area was often too small for complex configurations. RFC 1084 and later RFC 1533 expanded the vendor extensions, ultimately evolving into the comprehensive DHCP option space.
sections.plainLanguage: BOOTP has a 64-byte vendor-specific area for extra configuration, such as the subnet mask, default gateway, DNS server, hostname and domain name. This mechanism was later formalized as BOOTP options and became the basis for DHCP options. The 64 bytes were often too small, so RFC 1084 and RFC 1533 expanded the extensions.

subtitle: How a diskless workstation learns its IP address, its server and its boot file in one UDP exchange.

tldr.problem: A diskless client knows only its hardware address, and it needs an IP address, a server address and a boot file name before it can load a program.
tldr.mechanism: The client broadcasts a UDP BOOTREQUEST from port 68 to port 67, and a server looks the hardware address up in its database and answers with a BOOTREPLY that fills in the client's IP address, the server address and the boot file name.
tldr.outcome: BOOTP ran over ordinary UDP and could cross gateways, which RARP could not. Its packet layout and vendor area grew into DHCP.

plainLanguage.summary: BOOTP lets a diskless machine find its IP address, a server's address and a boot file name by broadcasting one request over UDP. Relay agents let a single server serve many network segments, which RARP could not do. BOOTP was later superseded by DHCP.

questions: what is the difference between bootp and rarp
how does a bootp relay agent work
how is bootp related to dhcp
today: Plain BOOTP is rare now, because DHCP (RFC 2131) uses nearly the same packet layout and the same UDP ports, 67 and 68, and adds dynamic addresses and leases. BOOTP is still alive in two ways: DHCP servers and relay agents commonly answer old BOOTP clients, and network boot firmware such as PXE builds on the same ideas of an address, a server and a boot file name. Packet analyzers such as Wireshark decode both protocols with the same field names.

messages.label: BOOTREQUEST (op = 1)
messages.note: UDP port 68 to port 67, usually to 255.255.255.255. Carries the client's hardware address in chaddr and its IP address in ciaddr if it knows one, otherwise zero.

messages.label: BOOTREPLY (op = 2)
messages.note: UDP destination port 68. Fills in yiaddr (the client's IP address), siaddr (the server's address) and file (the full boot file path name).

viz.caption: BOOTP packet, carried inside a UDP datagram

fields.name: op
fields.desc: Packet op code and message type: 1 = BOOTREQUEST, 2 = BOOTREPLY.

fields.name: htype
fields.desc: Hardware address type, from the ARP section of Assigned Numbers. 1 = 10 Mb Ethernet.

fields.name: hlen
fields.desc: Hardware address length, for example 6 for 10 Mb Ethernet.

fields.name: hops
fields.desc: Client sets this to zero. Gateways may use it in cross-gateway booting.

fields.name: xid
fields.desc: Transaction ID, a random number that matches a request with the replies it generates.

fields.name: secs
fields.desc: Filled in by the client: seconds elapsed since it started trying to boot.

fields.name: ciaddr
fields.desc: Client IP address, filled in by the client in a request if it is known.

fields.name: yiaddr
fields.desc: "Your" (client) IP address, filled in by the server if the client did not know its own address.

fields.name: siaddr
fields.desc: Server IP address, returned in the reply by the server.

fields.name: giaddr
fields.desc: Gateway IP address, used in optional cross-gateway booting.

fields.name: chaddr
fields.desc: Client hardware address, filled in by the client (16 octets).

fields.name: sname
fields.desc: Optional server host name, a null-terminated string (64 octets).

fields.name: file
fields.desc: Boot file name, a null-terminated string (128 octets). A generic name or null in a request, a fully qualified path name in the reply.

messages.label: BOOTREQUEST (broadcast)
messages.note: The client does nothing special; giaddr is still zero.

messages.label: Forwarded BOOTREQUEST
messages.note: If giaddr is zero the gateway puts its own address on the receiving cable there, and may increment hops.

messages.label: BOOTREPLY to giaddr, port 67
messages.note: The server sends the reply to the address in giaddr.

messages.label: BOOTREPLY to client, port 68
messages.note: The gateway delivers it on the client's cable.
